# Metallic mean

- [Español](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%BAmero_met%C3%A1lico)
- [Français](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nombre_m%C3%A9tallique)
- [Galego](https://gl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media_met%C3%A1lica)
- [日本語](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E8%B2%B4%E9%87%91%E5%B1%9E%E6%AF%94)
- [Latina](https://la.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratio_metallica)
- [Polski](https://pl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podzia%C5%82y_metaliczne)
- [Português](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A9dia_met%C3%A1lica)
- [粵語](https://zh-yue.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E8%B2%B4%E9%87%91%E5%B1%AC%E6%AF%94)
- [中文](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E8%B2%B4%E9%87%91%E5%B1%AC%E6%AF%94%E4%BE%8B)
 [Edit links](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Special:EntityPage/Q11634820#sitelinks-wikipedia)                          From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia   Generalization of golden and silver ratios [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/Fibonacci_spiral_34.svg/250px-Fibonacci_spiral_34.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fibonacci_spiral_34.svg)[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Silver_spiral_approximation.svg/250px-Silver_spiral_approximation.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Silver_spiral_approximation.svg)[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/Bronze_spiral_approximation.png/250px-Bronze_spiral_approximation.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bronze_spiral_approximation.png)Gold, silver, and bronze ratios within their respective rectangles.

The **metallic mean** (also **metallic ratio**, **metallic constant**, or **noble mean**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_mean#cite_note-1)) of a [natural number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_number) n is a positive [real number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number), denoted here      S  n   ,   {\displaystyle S_{n},}   that satisfies the following equivalent characterizations:

- the unique positive real number     x   {\displaystyle x}   such that     x = n +   1 x     {\textstyle x=n+{\frac {1}{x}}}
- the positive root of the [quadratic equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_equation)      x  2   − n x − 1 = 0   {\displaystyle x^{2}-nx-1=0}
- the number        n +    n  2   + 4    2   =   2     n  2   + 4   − n      {\textstyle {\frac {n+{\sqrt {n^{2}+4}}}{2}}={\frac {2}{{\sqrt {n^{2}+4}}-n}}}
- the number whose expression as a [continued fraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continued_fraction) is     [ n ; n , n , n , n , … ] = n +         1          n +         1          n +         1          n +         1          n + ⋱                        {\displaystyle [n;n,n,n,n,\dots ]=n+{\cfrac {1}{n+{\cfrac {1}{n+{\cfrac {1}{n+{\cfrac {1}{n+\ddots \,}}}}}}}}}

Metallic means are (successive) derivations of the [golden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_ratio) (    n = 1   {\displaystyle n=1}  ) and [silver ratios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_ratio) (    n = 2   {\displaystyle n=2}  ), and share some of their interesting properties. The term "bronze ratio" (    n = 3   {\displaystyle n=3}  ) (cf. [Golden Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Age) and [Olympic Medals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Medals)) and even metals such as copper (    n = 4   {\displaystyle n=4}  ) and nickel (    n = 5   {\displaystyle n=5}  ) are occasionally found in the literature.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_mean#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_mean#cite_note-3)[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_mean#cite_note-Note01-4)

In terms of [algebraic number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_theory), the metallic means are exactly the real [quadratic integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_integer) that are greater than     1   {\displaystyle 1}   and have     − 1   {\displaystyle -1}   as their [norm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_integer#Norm_and_conjugation).

The defining equation      x  2   − n x − 1 = 0   {\displaystyle x^{2}-nx-1=0}   of the nth metallic mean is the [characteristic equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_recurrence_relation#Characteristic_polynomial_and_roots) of a [linear recurrence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_recurrence_relation) of the form      x  k   = n  x  k − 1   +  x  k − 2   .   {\displaystyle x_{k}=nx_{k-1}+x_{k-2}.}   It follows that, given such a recurrence the solution can be expressed as

      x  k   = a  S  n   k   + b   (    − 1   S  n     )   k   ,   {\displaystyle x_{k}=aS_{n}^{k}+b\left({\frac {-1}{S_{n}}}\right)^{k},}

where      S  n     {\displaystyle S_{n}}   is the nth metallic mean, and a and b are constants depending only on      x  0     {\displaystyle x_{0}}   and      x  1   .   {\displaystyle x_{1}.}   Since the inverse of a metallic mean is less than 1, this formula implies that the quotient of two consecutive elements of such a sequence tends to the metallic mean, when k tends to the infinity.

For example, if     n = 1 ,   {\displaystyle n=1,}        S  n     {\displaystyle S_{n}}   is the [golden ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_ratio). If      x  0   = 0   {\displaystyle x_{0}=0}   and      x  1   = 1 ,   {\displaystyle x_{1}=1,}   the sequence is the [Fibonacci sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibonacci_sequence), and the above formula is [Binet's formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binet's_formula). If     n = 1 ,  x  0   = 2 ,  x  1   = 1   {\displaystyle n=1,x_{0}=2,x_{1}=1}   one has the [Lucas numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_number). If     n = 2 ,   {\displaystyle n=2,}   the metallic mean is called the [silver ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_ratio), and the elements of the sequence starting with      x  0   = 0   {\displaystyle x_{0}=0}   and      x  1   = 1   {\displaystyle x_{1}=1}   are called the [Pell numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pell_number).

## Geometry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Metallic_mean&action=edit&section=1)] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/Gold%2C_silver%2C_and_bronze_rectangles.svg/250px-Gold%2C_silver%2C_and_bronze_rectangles.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gold,_silver,_and_bronze_rectangles.svg)If one removes n largest possible squares from a rectangle with ratio length/width equal to the nth metallic mean, one gets a rectangle with the same ratio length/width (in the figures, n is the number of dotted lines). [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/Pentagram-phi.svg/250px-Pentagram-phi.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pentagram-phi.svg)[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Silver_ratio_octagon.svg/250px-Silver_ratio_octagon.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Silver_ratio_octagon.svg)Golden ratio within the pentagram (*φ* = red/ green = green/blue = blue/purple) and silver ratio within the octagon.

The defining equation     x = n +   1 x     {\textstyle x=n+{\frac {1}{x}}}   of the nth metallic mean induces the following geometrical interpretation.

Consider a [rectangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectangle) such that the ratio of its length L to its width W is the nth metallic ratio. If one remove from this rectangle n squares of side length W, one gets a rectangle [similar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Similarity_(geometry)) to the original rectangle; that is, a rectangle with the same ratio of the length to the width (see figures).

Some metallic means appear as [segments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_segment) in the figure formed by a [regular polygon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_polygon) and its diagonals. This is in particular the case for the [golden ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_ratio) and the [pentagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentagon), and for the [silver ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_ratio) and the [octagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octagon); see figures.

## Powers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Metallic_mean&action=edit&section=2)] [![icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg)This section **does not [cite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources) any [sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability)**. Please help [improve this section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:EditPage/Metallic_mean) by [adding citations to reliable sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Referencing_for_beginners). Unsourced material may be challenged and [removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Burden_of_evidence). *(August 2020)**([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal))*

Denoting by      S  m     {\displaystyle S_{m}}   the metallic mean of *m* one has

      S  m   n   =  K  n    S  m   +  K  n − 1   ,   {\displaystyle S_{m}^{n}=K_{n}S_{m}+K_{n-1},}

where the numbers      K  n     {\displaystyle K_{n}}   are defined [recursively](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_induction) by the initial conditions *K*0 = 0 and *K*1 = 1, and the [recurrence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrence_relation)

      K  n   = m  K  n − 1   +  K  n − 2   .   {\displaystyle K_{n}=mK_{n-1}+K_{n-2}.}

*Proof:* The equality is immediately true for     n = 1.   {\displaystyle n=1.}   The recurrence relation implies      K  2   = m ,   {\displaystyle K_{2}=m,}   which makes the equality true for     k = 2.   {\displaystyle k=2.}   Supposing the equality true up to     n − 1 ,   {\displaystyle n-1,}   one has

          S  m   n      = m  S  m   n − 1   +  S  m   n − 2       (defining equation)        = m (  K  n − 1    S  n   +  K  n − 2   ) + (  K  n − 2    S  m   +  K  n − 3   )     (recurrence hypothesis)        = ( m  K  n − 1   +  K  n − 2   )  S  n   + ( m  K  n − 2   +  K  n − 3   )     (regrouping)        =  K  n    S  m   +  K  n − 1       (recurrence on    K  n   ) .       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}S_{m}^{n}&=mS_{m}^{n-1}+S_{m}^{n-2}&&{\text{(defining equation)}}\\&=m(K_{n-1}S_{n}+K_{n-2})+(K_{n-2}S_{m}+K_{n-3})&&{\text{(recurrence hypothesis)}}\\&=(mK_{n-1}+K_{n-2})S_{n}+(mK_{n-2}+K_{n-3})&&{\text{(regrouping)}}\\&=K_{n}S_{m}+K_{n-1}&&{\text{(recurrence on }}K_{n}).\end{aligned}}}

*End of the proof.*

One has also [*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed)*]

      K  n   =     S  m   n + 1   − ( m −  S  m    )  n + 1      m  2   + 4    .   {\displaystyle K_{n}={\frac {S_{m}^{n+1}-(m-S_{m})^{n+1}}{\sqrt {m^{2}+4}}}.}

The odd powers of a metallic mean are themselves metallic means. More precisely, if n is an odd natural number, then      S  m   n   =  S   M  n     ,   {\displaystyle S_{m}^{n}=S_{M_{n}},}   where      M  n     {\displaystyle M_{n}}   is defined by the recurrence relation      M  n   = m  M  n − 1   +  M  n − 2     {\displaystyle M_{n}=mM_{n-1}+M_{n-2}}   and the initial conditions      M  0   = 2   {\displaystyle M_{0}=2}   and      M  1   = m .   {\displaystyle M_{1}=m.}

*Proof:* Let     a =  S  m     {\displaystyle a=S_{m}}   and     b = − 1  /   S  m   .   {\displaystyle b=-1/S_{m}.}   The definition of metallic means implies that     a + b = m   {\displaystyle a+b=m}   and     a b = − 1.   {\displaystyle ab=-1.}   Let      M  n   =  a  n   +  b  n   .   {\displaystyle M_{n}=a^{n}+b^{n}.}   Since      a  n    b  n   = ( a b  )  n   = − 1   {\displaystyle a^{n}b^{n}=(ab)^{n}=-1}   if n is odd, the power      a  n     {\displaystyle a^{n}}   is a root of      x  2   −  M  n   − 1 = 0.   {\displaystyle x^{2}-M_{n}-1=0.}   So, it remains to prove that      M  n     {\displaystyle M_{n}}   is an integer that satisfies the given recurrence relation. This results from the identity

          a  n   +  b  n      = ( a + b ) (  a  n − 1   +  b  n − 1   ) − a b (  a  n − 2   +  a  n − 2   )       = m (  a  n − 1   +  b  n − 1   ) + (  a  n − 2   +  a  n − 2   ) .       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}a^{n}+b^{n}&=(a+b)(a^{n-1}+b^{n-1})-ab(a^{n-2}+a^{n-2})\\&=m(a^{n-1}+b^{n-1})+(a^{n-2}+a^{n-2}).\end{aligned}}}

*This completes the proof,* given that the initial values are easy to verify.

In particular, one has

          S  m   3      =  S   m  3   + 3 m        S  m   5      =  S   m  5   + 5  m  3   + 5 m        S  m   7      =  S   m  7   + 7  m  5   + 14  m  3   + 7 m        S  m   9      =  S   m  9   + 9  m  7   + 27  m  5   + 30  m  3   + 9 m        S  m   11      =  S   m  11   + 11  m  9   + 44  m  7   + 77  m  5   + 55  m  3   + 11 m         {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}S_{m}^{3}&=S_{m^{3}+3m}\\S_{m}^{5}&=S_{m^{5}+5m^{3}+5m}\\S_{m}^{7}&=S_{m^{7}+7m^{5}+14m^{3}+7m}\\S_{m}^{9}&=S_{m^{9}+9m^{7}+27m^{5}+30m^{3}+9m}\\S_{m}^{11}&=S_{m^{11}+11m^{9}+44m^{7}+77m^{5}+55m^{3}+11m}\end{aligned}}}

and, in general,[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed)*]

      S  m   2 n + 1   =  S  M   ,   {\displaystyle S_{m}^{2n+1}=S_{M},}

where

     M =  ∑  k = 0   n      2 n + 1   2 k + 1       (    n + k   2 k    )     m  2 k + 1   .   {\displaystyle M=\sum _{k=0}^{n}{{2n+1} \over {2k+1}}{{n+k} \choose {2k}}m^{2k+1}.}

For even powers, things are more complicated. If *n* is a positive even integer then[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed)*]

       S  m   n   −  ⌊  S  m   n   ⌋   = 1 −  S  m   − n   .   {\displaystyle {S_{m}^{n}-\left\lfloor S_{m}^{n}\right\rfloor }=1-S_{m}^{-n}.}

Additionally,[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed)*]

       1   S  m   4   −  ⌊  S  m   4   ⌋     +  ⌊   S  m   4   − 1  ⌋  =  S   (   m  4   + 4  m  2   + 1  )      {\displaystyle {1 \over {S_{m}^{4}-\left\lfloor S_{m}^{4}\right\rfloor }}+\left\lfloor S_{m}^{4}-1\right\rfloor =S_{\left(m^{4}+4m^{2}+1\right)}}         1   S  m   6   −  ⌊  S  m   6   ⌋     +  ⌊   S  m   6   − 1  ⌋  =  S   (   m  6   + 6  m  4   + 9  m  2   + 1  )    .   {\displaystyle {1 \over {S_{m}^{6}-\left\lfloor S_{m}^{6}\right\rfloor }}+\left\lfloor S_{m}^{6}-1\right\rfloor =S_{\left(m^{6}+6m^{4}+9m^{2}+1\right)}.}

For the square of a metallic ratio we have:     S  m   2   = [ m    m  2   + 4   + ( m + 2 ) ]  /  2 = ( p +    p  2   + 4   )  /  2   {\displaystyle S_{m}^{2}=[m{\sqrt {m^{2}+4}}+(m+2)]/2=(p+{\sqrt {p^{2}+4}})/2}

where     p = m    m  2   + 4     {\displaystyle p=m{\sqrt {m^{2}+4}}}   lies strictly between      m  2   + 1   {\displaystyle m^{2}+1}   and      m  2   + 2   {\displaystyle m^{2}+2}  . Therefore

S   m  2   + 1   <  S  m   2   <  S   m  2   + 2     {\displaystyle S_{m^{2}+1}<S_{m}^{2}<S_{m^{2}+2}}

## Generalization

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Metallic_mean&action=edit&section=3)]

One may define the metallic mean      S  − n     {\displaystyle S_{-n}}   of a negative integer −*n* as the positive solution of the equation      x  2   − ( − n ) x − 1.   {\displaystyle x^{2}-(-n)x-1.}   The metallic mean of −*n* is the [multiplicative inverse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplicative_inverse) of the metallic mean of *n*:

      S  − n   =   1  S  n     .   {\displaystyle S_{-n}={\frac {1}{S_{n}}}.}

Another generalization consists of changing the defining equation from      x  2   − n x − 1 = 0   {\displaystyle x^{2}-nx-1=0}   to      x  2   − n x − c = 0   {\displaystyle x^{2}-nx-c=0}  . If

     R =    n ±    n  2   + 4 c    2   ,   {\displaystyle R={\frac {n\pm {\sqrt {n^{2}+4c}}}{2}},}

is any root of the equation, one has

     R − n =   c R   .   {\displaystyle R-n={\frac {c}{R}}.}

The silver mean of *m* is also given by the integral[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_mean#cite_note-:0-5)

      S  m   =  ∫  0   m     (    x  2    x  2   + 4      +    m + 2   2 m     )    d x .   {\displaystyle S_{m}=\int _{0}^{m}{\left({x \over {2{\sqrt {x^{2}+4}}}}+{{m+2} \over {2m}}\right)}\,dx.}

Another form of the metallic mean is[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_mean#cite_note-:0-5)

        n +    n  2   + 4    2   =  e   a r s i n h ( n  /  2 )    .   {\displaystyle {\frac {n+{\sqrt {n^{2}+4}}}{2}}=e^{\operatorname {arsinh(n/2)} }.}

## Relation to half-angle cotangent

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Metallic_mean&action=edit&section=4)]

A [tangent half-angle formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent_half-angle_formula) gives     cot ⁡ θ =     cot  2   ⁡   θ 2   − 1   2 cot ⁡   θ 2        {\displaystyle \cot \theta ={\frac {\cot ^{2}{\frac {\theta }{2}}-1}{2\cot {\frac {\theta }{2}}}}}   which can be rewritten as      cot  2   ⁡   θ 2   − ( 2 cot ⁡ θ ) cot ⁡   θ 2   − 1 = 0  .   {\displaystyle \cot ^{2}{\frac {\theta }{2}}-(2\cot \theta )\cot {\frac {\theta }{2}}-1=0\,.}   That is, for the positive value of     cot ⁡   θ 2     {\textstyle \cot {\frac {\theta }{2}}}  , the metallic mean      S  2 cot ⁡ θ   = cot ⁡   θ 2    ,   {\displaystyle S_{2\cot \theta }=\cot {\frac {\theta }{2}}\,,}   which is especially meaningful when     2 cot ⁡ θ   {\textstyle 2\cot \theta }   is a positive integer, as it is with some Pythagorean triangles.

## Relation to Pythagorean triples

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Metallic_mean&action=edit&section=5)] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/AgamRiaSanga.png/250px-AgamRiaSanga.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AgamRiaSanga.png)Metallic Ratios in Primitive Pythagorean Triangles

For a [primitive Pythagorean triple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primitive_Pythagorean_triple), *a*2 + *b*2 = *c*2, with positive integers *a* < *b* < *c* that are [relatively prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relatively_prime), if the difference between the [hypotenuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypotenuse) c and [longer leg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathetus) b is 1, 2 or 8 then the Pythagorean triangle exhibits a metallic mean. Specifically, the [cotangent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotangent) of one quarter of the smaller acute angle of the Pythagorean triangle is a metallic mean.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_mean#cite_note-6)

More precisely, for a primitive Pythagorean triple (*a*, *b*, *c*) with *a* < *b* < *c*, the smaller acute angle α satisfies     tan ⁡   α 2   =    c − b  a    .   {\displaystyle \tan {\frac {\alpha }{2}}={\frac {c-b}{a}}\,.}   When *c* − *b* ∈ {1, 2, 8}, we will always get that     n = 2 cot ⁡   α 2   =    2 a   c − b      {\displaystyle n=2\cot {\frac {\alpha }{2}}={\frac {2a}{c-b}}}   is an integer and that     cot ⁡   α 4   =  S  n    ,   {\displaystyle \cot {\frac {\alpha }{4}}=S_{n}\,,}   the n-th metallic mean.

The reverse direction also works. For *n* ≥ 5, the primitive Pythagorean triple that gives the n-th metallic mean is given by (*n*, *n*2/4 − 1, *n*2/4 + 1) if n is a multiple of 4, is given by (*n*/2, (*n*2 − 4)/8, (*n*2 + 4)/8) if n is even but not a multiple of 4, and is given by (4*n*, *n*2 − 4, *n*2 + 4) if n is odd. For example, the primitive Pythagorean triple (20, 21, 29) gives the 5th metallic mean; (3, 4, 5) gives the 6th metallic mean; (28, 45, 53) gives the 7th metallic mean; (8, 15, 17) gives the 8th metallic mean; and so on.

## Relation to Aperiodic Order

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Metallic_mean&action=edit&section=7)]

The     k   {\displaystyle k}  -th metallic mean serves as the inflation ratio for one-dimensional substitution tilings, such as     a →  a  k   b   {\displaystyle a\to a^{k}b}   and     b → a   {\displaystyle b\to a}  . These sequences exhibit long-range aperiodic order. By applying an interval removal process to these tilings, one can construct self-similar Cantor sets where the Hausdorff dimension is determined by the metallic mean scaling factor.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_mean#cite_note-20)

Metallic mean

# Metallic mean

 [Edit links](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Special:EntityPage/Q11634820#sitelinks-wikipedia)                          From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia   Generalization of golden and silver ratios [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/Fibonacci_spiral_34.svg/250px-Fibonacci_spiral_34.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fibonacci_spiral_34.svg)[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Silver_spiral_approximation.svg/250px-Silver_spiral_approximation.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Silver_spiral_approximation.svg)[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/Bronze_spiral_approximation.png/250px-Bronze_spiral_approximation.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bronze_spiral_approximation.png)Gold, silver, and bronze ratios within their respective rectangles.

The **metallic mean** (also **metallic ratio**, **metallic constant**, or **noble mean**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_mean#cite_note-1)) of a [natural number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_number) n is a positive [real number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number), denoted here      S  n   ,   {\displaystyle S_{n},}   that satisfies the following equivalent characterizations:

- the unique positive real number     x   {\displaystyle x}   such that     x = n +   1 x     {\textstyle x=n+{\frac {1}{x}}}
- the positive root of the [quadratic equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_equation)      x  2   − n x − 1 = 0   {\displaystyle x^{2}-nx-1=0}
- the number        n +    n  2   + 4    2   =   2     n  2   + 4   − n      {\textstyle {\frac {n+{\sqrt {n^{2}+4}}}{2}}={\frac {2}{{\sqrt {n^{2}+4}}-n}}}
- the number whose expression as a [continued fraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continued_fraction) is     [ n ; n , n , n , n , … ] = n +         1          n +         1          n +         1          n +         1          n + ⋱                        {\displaystyle [n;n,n,n,n,\dots ]=n+{\cfrac {1}{n+{\cfrac {1}{n+{\cfrac {1}{n+{\cfrac {1}{n+\ddots \,}}}}}}}}}

Metallic means are (successive) derivations of the [golden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_ratio) (    n = 1   {\displaystyle n=1}  ) and [silver ratios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_ratio) (    n = 2   {\displaystyle n=2}  ), and share some of their interesting properties. The term "bronze ratio" (    n = 3   {\displaystyle n=3}  ) (cf. [Golden Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Age) and [Olympic Medals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Medals)) and even metals such as copper (    n = 4   {\displaystyle n=4}  ) and nickel (    n = 5   {\displaystyle n=5}  ) are occasionally found in the literature.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_mean#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_mean#cite_note-3)[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_mean#cite_note-Note01-4)

In terms of [algebraic number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_theory), the metallic means are exactly the real [quadratic integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_integer) that are greater than     1   {\displaystyle 1}   and have     − 1   {\displaystyle -1}   as their [norm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_integer#Norm_and_conjugation).

The defining equation      x  2   − n x − 1 = 0   {\displaystyle x^{2}-nx-1=0}   of the nth metallic mean is the [characteristic equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_recurrence_relation#Characteristic_polynomial_and_roots) of a [linear recurrence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_recurrence_relation) of the form      x  k   = n  x  k − 1   +  x  k − 2   .   {\displaystyle x_{k}=nx_{k-1}+x_{k-2}.}   It follows that, given such a recurrence the solution can be expressed as

      x  k   = a  S  n   k   + b   (    − 1   S  n     )   k   ,   {\displaystyle x_{k}=aS_{n}^{k}+b\left({\frac {-1}{S_{n}}}\right)^{k},}

where      S  n     {\displaystyle S_{n}}   is the nth metallic mean, and a and b are constants depending only on      x  0     {\displaystyle x_{0}}   and      x  1   .   {\displaystyle x_{1}.}   Since the inverse of a metallic mean is less than 1, this formula implies that the quotient of two consecutive elements of such a sequence tends to the metallic mean, when k tends to the infinity.

For example, if     n = 1 ,   {\displaystyle n=1,}        S  n     {\displaystyle S_{n}}   is the [golden ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_ratio). If      x  0   = 0   {\displaystyle x_{0}=0}   and      x  1   = 1 ,   {\displaystyle x_{1}=1,}   the sequence is the [Fibonacci sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibonacci_sequence), and the above formula is [Binet's formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binet's_formula). If     n = 1 ,  x  0   = 2 ,  x  1   = 1   {\displaystyle n=1,x_{0}=2,x_{1}=1}   one has the [Lucas numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_number). If     n = 2 ,   {\displaystyle n=2,}   the metallic mean is called the [silver ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_ratio), and the elements of the sequence starting with      x  0   = 0   {\displaystyle x_{0}=0}   and      x  1   = 1   {\displaystyle x_{1}=1}   are called the [Pell numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pell_number).

Geometry

# Geometry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Metallic_mean&action=edit&section=1)] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/Gold%2C_silver%2C_and_bronze_rectangles.svg/250px-Gold%2C_silver%2C_and_bronze_rectangles.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gold,_silver,_and_bronze_rectangles.svg)If one removes n largest possible squares from a rectangle with ratio length/width equal to the nth metallic mean, one gets a rectangle with the same ratio length/width (in the figures, n is the number of dotted lines). [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/Pentagram-phi.svg/250px-Pentagram-phi.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pentagram-phi.svg)[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Silver_ratio_octagon.svg/250px-Silver_ratio_octagon.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Silver_ratio_octagon.svg)Golden ratio within the pentagram (*φ* = red/ green = green/blue = blue/purple) and silver ratio within the octagon.

The defining equation     x = n +   1 x     {\textstyle x=n+{\frac {1}{x}}}   of the nth metallic mean induces the following geometrical interpretation.

Consider a [rectangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectangle) such that the ratio of its length L to its width W is the nth metallic ratio. If one remove from this rectangle n squares of side length W, one gets a rectangle [similar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Similarity_(geometry)) to the original rectangle; that is, a rectangle with the same ratio of the length to the width (see figures).

Some metallic means appear as [segments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_segment) in the figure formed by a [regular polygon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_polygon) and its diagonals. This is in particular the case for the [golden ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_ratio) and the [pentagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentagon), and for the [silver ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_ratio) and the [octagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octagon); see figures.

Powers

# Powers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Metallic_mean&action=edit&section=2)] [![icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg)This section **does not [cite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources) any [sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability)**. Please help [improve this section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:EditPage/Metallic_mean) by [adding citations to reliable sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Referencing_for_beginners). Unsourced material may be challenged and [removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Burden_of_evidence). *(August 2020)**([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal))*

Denoting by      S  m     {\displaystyle S_{m}}   the metallic mean of *m* one has

      S  m   n   =  K  n    S  m   +  K  n − 1   ,   {\displaystyle S_{m}^{n}=K_{n}S_{m}+K_{n-1},}

where the numbers      K  n     {\displaystyle K_{n}}   are defined [recursively](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_induction) by the initial conditions *K*0 = 0 and *K*1 = 1, and the [recurrence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrence_relation)

      K  n   = m  K  n − 1   +  K  n − 2   .   {\displaystyle K_{n}=mK_{n-1}+K_{n-2}.}

*Proof:* The equality is immediately true for     n = 1.   {\displaystyle n=1.}   The recurrence relation implies      K  2   = m ,   {\displaystyle K_{2}=m,}   which makes the equality true for     k = 2.   {\displaystyle k=2.}   Supposing the equality true up to     n − 1 ,   {\displaystyle n-1,}   one has

          S  m   n      = m  S  m   n − 1   +  S  m   n − 2       (defining equation)        = m (  K  n − 1    S  n   +  K  n − 2   ) + (  K  n − 2    S  m   +  K  n − 3   )     (recurrence hypothesis)        = ( m  K  n − 1   +  K  n − 2   )  S  n   + ( m  K  n − 2   +  K  n − 3   )     (regrouping)        =  K  n    S  m   +  K  n − 1       (recurrence on    K  n   ) .       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}S_{m}^{n}&=mS_{m}^{n-1}+S_{m}^{n-2}&&{\text{(defining equation)}}\\&=m(K_{n-1}S_{n}+K_{n-2})+(K_{n-2}S_{m}+K_{n-3})&&{\text{(recurrence hypothesis)}}\\&=(mK_{n-1}+K_{n-2})S_{n}+(mK_{n-2}+K_{n-3})&&{\text{(regrouping)}}\\&=K_{n}S_{m}+K_{n-1}&&{\text{(recurrence on }}K_{n}).\end{aligned}}}

*End of the proof.*

One has also [*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed)*]

      K  n   =     S  m   n + 1   − ( m −  S  m    )  n + 1      m  2   + 4    .   {\displaystyle K_{n}={\frac {S_{m}^{n+1}-(m-S_{m})^{n+1}}{\sqrt {m^{2}+4}}}.}

The odd powers of a metallic mean are themselves metallic means. More precisely, if n is an odd natural number, then      S  m   n   =  S   M  n     ,   {\displaystyle S_{m}^{n}=S_{M_{n}},}   where      M  n     {\displaystyle M_{n}}   is defined by the recurrence relation      M  n   = m  M  n − 1   +  M  n − 2     {\displaystyle M_{n}=mM_{n-1}+M_{n-2}}   and the initial conditions      M  0   = 2   {\displaystyle M_{0}=2}   and      M  1   = m .   {\displaystyle M_{1}=m.}

*Proof:* Let     a =  S  m     {\displaystyle a=S_{m}}   and     b = − 1  /   S  m   .   {\displaystyle b=-1/S_{m}.}   The definition of metallic means implies that     a + b = m   {\displaystyle a+b=m}   and     a b = − 1.   {\displaystyle ab=-1.}   Let      M  n   =  a  n   +  b  n   .   {\displaystyle M_{n}=a^{n}+b^{n}.}   Since      a  n    b  n   = ( a b  )  n   = − 1   {\displaystyle a^{n}b^{n}=(ab)^{n}=-1}   if n is odd, the power      a  n     {\displaystyle a^{n}}   is a root of      x  2   −  M  n   − 1 = 0.   {\displaystyle x^{2}-M_{n}-1=0.}   So, it remains to prove that      M  n     {\displaystyle M_{n}}   is an integer that satisfies the given recurrence relation. This results from the identity

          a  n   +  b  n      = ( a + b ) (  a  n − 1   +  b  n − 1   ) − a b (  a  n − 2   +  a  n − 2   )       = m (  a  n − 1   +  b  n − 1   ) + (  a  n − 2   +  a  n − 2   ) .       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}a^{n}+b^{n}&=(a+b)(a^{n-1}+b^{n-1})-ab(a^{n-2}+a^{n-2})\\&=m(a^{n-1}+b^{n-1})+(a^{n-2}+a^{n-2}).\end{aligned}}}

*This completes the proof,* given that the initial values are easy to verify.

In particular, one has

          S  m   3      =  S   m  3   + 3 m        S  m   5      =  S   m  5   + 5  m  3   + 5 m        S  m   7      =  S   m  7   + 7  m  5   + 14  m  3   + 7 m        S  m   9      =  S   m  9   + 9  m  7   + 27  m  5   + 30  m  3   + 9 m        S  m   11      =  S   m  11   + 11  m  9   + 44  m  7   + 77  m  5   + 55  m  3   + 11 m         {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}S_{m}^{3}&=S_{m^{3}+3m}\\S_{m}^{5}&=S_{m^{5}+5m^{3}+5m}\\S_{m}^{7}&=S_{m^{7}+7m^{5}+14m^{3}+7m}\\S_{m}^{9}&=S_{m^{9}+9m^{7}+27m^{5}+30m^{3}+9m}\\S_{m}^{11}&=S_{m^{11}+11m^{9}+44m^{7}+77m^{5}+55m^{3}+11m}\end{aligned}}}

and, in general,[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed)*]

      S  m   2 n + 1   =  S  M   ,   {\displaystyle S_{m}^{2n+1}=S_{M},}

where

     M =  ∑  k = 0   n      2 n + 1   2 k + 1       (    n + k   2 k    )     m  2 k + 1   .   {\displaystyle M=\sum _{k=0}^{n}{{2n+1} \over {2k+1}}{{n+k} \choose {2k}}m^{2k+1}.}

For even powers, things are more complicated. If *n* is a positive even integer then[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed)*]

       S  m   n   −  ⌊  S  m   n   ⌋   = 1 −  S  m   − n   .   {\displaystyle {S_{m}^{n}-\left\lfloor S_{m}^{n}\right\rfloor }=1-S_{m}^{-n}.}

Additionally,[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed)*]

       1   S  m   4   −  ⌊  S  m   4   ⌋     +  ⌊   S  m   4   − 1  ⌋  =  S   (   m  4   + 4  m  2   + 1  )      {\displaystyle {1 \over {S_{m}^{4}-\left\lfloor S_{m}^{4}\right\rfloor }}+\left\lfloor S_{m}^{4}-1\right\rfloor =S_{\left(m^{4}+4m^{2}+1\right)}}         1   S  m   6   −  ⌊  S  m   6   ⌋     +  ⌊   S  m   6   − 1  ⌋  =  S   (   m  6   + 6  m  4   + 9  m  2   + 1  )    .   {\displaystyle {1 \over {S_{m}^{6}-\left\lfloor S_{m}^{6}\right\rfloor }}+\left\lfloor S_{m}^{6}-1\right\rfloor =S_{\left(m^{6}+6m^{4}+9m^{2}+1\right)}.}

For the square of a metallic ratio we have:     S  m   2   = [ m    m  2   + 4   + ( m + 2 ) ]  /  2 = ( p +    p  2   + 4   )  /  2   {\displaystyle S_{m}^{2}=[m{\sqrt {m^{2}+4}}+(m+2)]/2=(p+{\sqrt {p^{2}+4}})/2}

where     p = m    m  2   + 4     {\displaystyle p=m{\sqrt {m^{2}+4}}}   lies strictly between      m  2   + 1   {\displaystyle m^{2}+1}   and      m  2   + 2   {\displaystyle m^{2}+2}  . Therefore

S   m  2   + 1   <  S  m   2   <  S   m  2   + 2     {\displaystyle S_{m^{2}+1}<S_{m}^{2}<S_{m^{2}+2}}

Generalization

# Generalization

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Metallic_mean&action=edit&section=3)]

One may define the metallic mean      S  − n     {\displaystyle S_{-n}}   of a negative integer −*n* as the positive solution of the equation      x  2   − ( − n ) x − 1.   {\displaystyle x^{2}-(-n)x-1.}   The metallic mean of −*n* is the [multiplicative inverse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplicative_inverse) of the metallic mean of *n*:

      S  − n   =   1  S  n     .   {\displaystyle S_{-n}={\frac {1}{S_{n}}}.}

Another generalization consists of changing the defining equation from      x  2   − n x − 1 = 0   {\displaystyle x^{2}-nx-1=0}   to      x  2   − n x − c = 0   {\displaystyle x^{2}-nx-c=0}  . If

     R =    n ±    n  2   + 4 c    2   ,   {\displaystyle R={\frac {n\pm {\sqrt {n^{2}+4c}}}{2}},}

is any root of the equation, one has

     R − n =   c R   .   {\displaystyle R-n={\frac {c}{R}}.}

The silver mean of *m* is also given by the integral[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_mean#cite_note-:0-5)

      S  m   =  ∫  0   m     (    x  2    x  2   + 4      +    m + 2   2 m     )    d x .   {\displaystyle S_{m}=\int _{0}^{m}{\left({x \over {2{\sqrt {x^{2}+4}}}}+{{m+2} \over {2m}}\right)}\,dx.}

Another form of the metallic mean is[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_mean#cite_note-:0-5)

        n +    n  2   + 4    2   =  e   a r s i n h ( n  /  2 )    .   {\displaystyle {\frac {n+{\sqrt {n^{2}+4}}}{2}}=e^{\operatorname {arsinh(n/2)} }.}

Relation to half-angle cotangent

# Relation to half-angle cotangent

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Metallic_mean&action=edit&section=4)]

A [tangent half-angle formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent_half-angle_formula) gives     cot ⁡ θ =     cot  2   ⁡   θ 2   − 1   2 cot ⁡   θ 2        {\displaystyle \cot \theta ={\frac {\cot ^{2}{\frac {\theta }{2}}-1}{2\cot {\frac {\theta }{2}}}}}   which can be rewritten as      cot  2   ⁡   θ 2   − ( 2 cot ⁡ θ ) cot ⁡   θ 2   − 1 = 0  .   {\displaystyle \cot ^{2}{\frac {\theta }{2}}-(2\cot \theta )\cot {\frac {\theta }{2}}-1=0\,.}   That is, for the positive value of     cot ⁡   θ 2     {\textstyle \cot {\frac {\theta }{2}}}  , the metallic mean      S  2 cot ⁡ θ   = cot ⁡   θ 2    ,   {\displaystyle S_{2\cot \theta }=\cot {\frac {\theta }{2}}\,,}   which is especially meaningful when     2 cot ⁡ θ   {\textstyle 2\cot \theta }   is a positive integer, as it is with some Pythagorean triangles.

Relation to Pythagorean triples

# Relation to Pythagorean triples

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Metallic_mean&action=edit&section=5)] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/AgamRiaSanga.png/250px-AgamRiaSanga.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AgamRiaSanga.png)Metallic Ratios in Primitive Pythagorean Triangles

For a [primitive Pythagorean triple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primitive_Pythagorean_triple), *a*2 + *b*2 = *c*2, with positive integers *a* < *b* < *c* that are [relatively prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relatively_prime), if the difference between the [hypotenuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypotenuse) c and [longer leg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathetus) b is 1, 2 or 8 then the Pythagorean triangle exhibits a metallic mean. Specifically, the [cotangent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotangent) of one quarter of the smaller acute angle of the Pythagorean triangle is a metallic mean.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_mean#cite_note-6)

More precisely, for a primitive Pythagorean triple (*a*, *b*, *c*) with *a* < *b* < *c*, the smaller acute angle α satisfies     tan ⁡   α 2   =    c − b  a    .   {\displaystyle \tan {\frac {\alpha }{2}}={\frac {c-b}{a}}\,.}   When *c* − *b* ∈ {1, 2, 8}, we will always get that     n = 2 cot ⁡   α 2   =    2 a   c − b      {\displaystyle n=2\cot {\frac {\alpha }{2}}={\frac {2a}{c-b}}}   is an integer and that     cot ⁡   α 4   =  S  n    ,   {\displaystyle \cot {\frac {\alpha }{4}}=S_{n}\,,}   the n-th metallic mean.

The reverse direction also works. For *n* ≥ 5, the primitive Pythagorean triple that gives the n-th metallic mean is given by (*n*, *n*2/4 − 1, *n*2/4 + 1) if n is a multiple of 4, is given by (*n*/2, (*n*2 − 4)/8, (*n*2 + 4)/8) if n is even but not a multiple of 4, and is given by (4*n*, *n*2 − 4, *n*2 + 4) if n is odd. For example, the primitive Pythagorean triple (20, 21, 29) gives the 5th metallic mean; (3, 4, 5) gives the 6th metallic mean; (28, 45, 53) gives the 7th metallic mean; (8, 15, 17) gives the 8th metallic mean; and so on.

Relation to Aperiodic Order

# Relation to Aperiodic Order

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Metallic_mean&action=edit&section=7)]

The     k   {\displaystyle k}  -th metallic mean serves as the inflation ratio for one-dimensional substitution tilings, such as     a →  a  k   b   {\displaystyle a\to a^{k}b}   and     b → a   {\displaystyle b\to a}  . These sequences exhibit long-range aperiodic order. By applying an interval removal process to these tilings, one can construct self-similar Cantor sets where the Hausdorff dimension is determined by the metallic mean scaling factor.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_mean#cite_note-20)
